speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to put a question to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources. Is it true that certain officials of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources are impeding the work of Catholic and Protestant missionaries in the far north and exerting a harmful influence against those missionaries?
(Text):

speakeroldname: Hon. Alvin Hamillon (Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subsubtopic: REPORTED INTERFERENCE WITH WORK OF MISSIONARIES
speechtext:
I want to thank the hon. member for approaching me before the house opened and indicating that he was going to ask this question.
In reply to the hon. member I should point out that for over a century the welfare of the Eskimos in the far north was looked after almost entirely by missionaries, by the R.C.M.P. and by the members of the Hudson's Bay Company. Only when it became clear to the government some years ago, with the fall-off of the cariboo and the other forms of wild life, that it was necessary for the government to go in and assist in education, health and welfare, did the government begin to move.
With regard to the question of education, about which this article is concerned, I should

Inquiries of the Ministry point out that some years ago the government of the day made a mutually satisfactory cooperative arrangement for residences for school children and for the operation of the schools in the north. This arrangement, worked out by my predecessor, Mr. Lesage, was for a school system without any racial lines whatsoever. This arrangement was arrived at after full discussions with the religious authorities of the Roman Catholic church and the Anglican church. It was taken up with the territorial council. They considered it, and they accepted this arrangement.
I want to make it perfectly clear as minister at the present time that there has been no change in that arrangement. Last year I raised the status of the Eskimo affairs committee to that of a full advisory board reporting to the minister. As minister I thought it was fitting to invite Eskimos to sit on this board and give their direct advice to the minister. Also on the board, deliberately, are representatives of both the Anglican church and the Roman Catholic church, which have missionaries in this area. The board also has members from the mounted police, the Hudson's Bay Company and the health and welfare services of the government.
This board does not meet until next week; therefore until it meets it has tendered nothing to me. Until it does tender something to me I have nothing to consider. Thus it can be recognized, Mr. Speaker, that this shockingly irresponsible article in the paper is, to say the least, premature.

speakeroldname: Hon. D. S. Harkness (Minister of Agriculture):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, knowing the epicurean
tastes of the hon. member I can appreciate his interest in snails. Permission to import snails from Europe for the establishment of a snail farm in British Columbia was denied under the authority of the Destructive Insect and Pest Act, to prevent the introduction into Canada of any insect, pest or disease destructive to vegetation. Non-payment of Income Tax by Hutterites section 62 of the Income Tax Act be so interpreted as to make the Hutterite colonies subject to income tax. I did not hear the hon. member advocate that any other religious communities should also be liable to the income tax laws of the dominion of Canada. I am not saying that the complaint of the hon. member for Acadia should not have attention paid to it. However, I know full well that the hon. member for Acadia did not at all realize the issue that he raised in this House of Commons. Otherwise, being the fair minded westerner that he usually is, I am sure he would have decided against using the chamber of this House of Commons for that purpose.
I hope that he was asking that all religious organizations in Canada be made subject to income tax payments on all their commercial undertakings. If that is what the hon. member was asking for, there is a great deal of merit in it. However, if he was asking that only the Hutterites be made subject to income tax, then I must rise in my place to raise strenuous objection. These people do not exercise the franchise. There are only 6,518 in Canada. This is according to information I have from a survey made in 1950 census of the Hutterites in North America and which indicate Canada as having 6,518 of them. These population figures in this table were made available by Dr. Robert Friedmann, department of history, western Michigan college of education. This is taken from a report called "The Hutterites and Saskatchewan", conducted by the Saskatchewan division of the Canadian Mental Health Association. I regard this as a very reputable organization.
I therefore feel that the loss involved to the treasury by the Hutterite colonies not paying income tax is not a great loss indeed. However, I would remind the hon. member that the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan), on behalf of Canada, is being denied potential tens of millions of dollars of income tax when much larger religious organizations are exempt on commercial enterprises that they operate. This consideration involves almost every religious community in Canada. I feel that it is most unfair and most uncharitable to look in Canada for a little minority that has never harmed anyone in Canada, on whom we spend practically no public money whatsoever, who do not break the laws of Canada, who have a higher mental health rate than the rest of Canada-and this is all in the report-people who want to exercise their religious views not merely by worshipping as they please but by living as they believe. To ask us to discriminate against a group of this kind and ask that they should have to pay income tax while other much

I would like to challenge the hon. member to explain why he complains of the operation of section 62 of the Income Tax Act, and why does he pick on the harmless Hutterites of Canada? Why does he not refer to some of the religious organizations who are avoiding, rightly or wrongly, legally or otherwise, payment of tens of millions of dollars of income tax in Canada?
On reading over what the hon. member had to say, his whole argument seemed to be that he was not so much concerned with a loss of revenue to the government. His main desire appeared to be to force these colonies to pay income tax, thereby limiting their ability to expand. I do not think I am doing the hon. member any wrong when I imply a motive of that kind. The whole tenor of his speech was to the effect that if these people have to pay income tax they will not have as much money as they otherwise would have for the purposes of expansion.
In that connection I should like to read from the report which has already been referred to, "The Hutterites and Saskatchewan", a quotation from an article written by George Yacqulic called "The Hutterite Problem", contained in the Toronto Saturday Night for September 6, 1952. It is as follows:
Some of them have 150 people living off the same acreage of land as operated by one or two large-scale neighbouring farmers who are non-Hutteries. One colony east of Lethbridge has 146 souls deriving their livelihood from 5,200 acres of farming and ranching land. Adjoining this colony is a farming empire operated by two brothers who annually raise wheat on more than 10,000 acres.
These people have an economic problem. As their population grows, so they have to obtain more land. The hon. member did not offer any answer as to how they might obtain more land without violating their religious beliefs.
Mr. Speaker, I believe that the problem is more one of plain envy on the part of a lot of Canadians. Here are people who do not own any personal property, who operate their farms as one community and who are tremendously successful from the point of view of making money. This is a case where practical democratic socialism is yielding far higher returns than the outworn capitalist method and their capitalist neighbours are green with envy at the success of the Hutterites in the economic field. Then they elect themselves a member to the House of Commons who appeals to the government of the day to levy income tax on this religious community while ignoring the


fact that all religious communities in Canada are receiving the blessings of section 62 of the Income Tax Act.
If the hon. member's concern does not involve the fact that this is a religious community, then we have some further reservations. Because if it is not to be regarded as a religious community, then certainly it has to be regarded as a co-operative. I would like to ask the hon. member whether he is advocating that the co-operatives of Canada be called upon to pay income tax the same as any individual? I would like to ask him why he has picked this one small religious community and ignored the larger ones? If it is not because of the fact that it is a religious community which is making money, if it is because they are an economic unit and therefore ought to be taxed, then will he say whether he is in favour of co-operatives in Canada paying income tax as do privately owned corporations?
I regret very much that the popular method in past Canadian history has been to use minorities, racial, religious or ethnical, as whipping boys; and I also submit that the House of Commons is not the proper place to deal with this matter. We can all make representations to the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan); and he has had many representations from my area concerning this very section of the Income Tax Act. There are many religious organizations in Ontario and British Columbia who are very concerned at the operation of section 62 of the Income Tax Act, but the place to obtain equity in this regard is not on the floor of this House of Commons.

-I might point out to those who are afraid that I might be going out to tax every religious corporation. I have no such thought in mind-

Some of the questions that some hon. members might ask are these. Who are the Hutterites in the first place? Why are they different from other residents of Canada? Are they really a social problem, and should they be given what appears to be preferred treatment in regard to taxation? I regret very deeply this most unwarranted attack on one of the most harmless minorities, if not the most harmless one that exists in Canada.

They are certainly making it very difficult for a lot of others to understand it, too.
The Hutterite group to which we have been referring was founded in 1526 in Switzerland. They were a group of Swiss pacifists. The Hutterite communities are the oldest communistic societies in the world. They actually practice communal living, a life of non-conformity to the rest of the world. They say they are not citizens of any country and those we are talking about claim not to be citizens of Canada.
In the late 1700's they migrated to Russia and to other eastern German states. In that same year Catherine the Great of Russia granted them, as immigrants, military exemption, freedom to control their own schools and exemption from taxation for only three years. They remained in Russia at that period for about one hundred years and became immensely wealthy. In 1870 Alexander II withdrew the privilege of military exemption from them. This caused uneasiness amongst them and in 1873 a delegation was sent to the United States to investigate the prospects of their moving to a new home in that country.
President Grant, who was president of the United States at that time, assured them they would be most welcome but that they would not be considered as a privileged group. There would be no exemption from military service and no tax concessions as far as President Grant was concerned. In spite of this they decided to move and came to North America in 1875. In 1898 the Spanish-American war loomed as a threat to their pacifist ideas and in addition public feeling started to rise against them in the United States at that time. It became very acute.
They sent a delegation to Canada to investigate the prospects of moving the colonies to this country and particularly to western Canada. The Canadian government encouraged that move. An agreement was reached under which the Hutterites by order in council were granted special privileges. In the spring of 1899 one colony only moved from the United States to southern Manitoba.
The Spanish-American war came to an end in that year and so the other colonies decided to remain in the United States. In 1905 the colony that had moved to Manitoba returned to the United States and thus there were no Hutterites in Canada from 1905 until about 1917.
World war I showed how unpopular their pacifist ideas were in the United States at that time. In 1917 the selective service act of the United States and the draft acts were enacted. The Hutterites with the pacifist

Non-payment of Income Tax by Hutterites concepts refused military service. As a consequence the leaders of the Hutterites again contacted the Canadian authorities. The Hon.
J.	A. Calder, minister of colonization and immigration at that time, gave them the assurance that if the Hutterites came to Canada they would be exempt from military service and would be granted special rights which would allow them freedom to continue their communal way of life. They were granted the right for holding property in common. Although this was under provincial jurisdiction the arrangements were made through federal agencies.
In 1918 the colonies emigrated from South Dakota to Montana and Alberta. At that time large protest meetings were held in Winnipeg, one of which was attended by 35,000 people. The people protested against the granting of preferred treatment to certain groups. As a result of those meetings the order in council to which I referred was rescinded.
There were 12 original groups which settled in Alberta in 1918. There are now established in Alberta 55 colonies and 10 additional colonies in Saskatchewan. The first colony entered Saskatchewan in 1952, only eight years ago. Since that time, 8 colonies have been established in my own constituency, some of these touching boundary to boundary. Four of them are located within an area of 30 miles.
As the hon. member for Acadia said last evening, the Hutterites live frugally and avoid everything that is in the nature of luxury. All of the profits from farming or ranching operations belong to the colony or the head of the colony. All surplus funds are used for one purpose only and that is to buy more land. When the population of any settlement increases beyond 100, or a unit as they call it, they consider dividing the establishment into a new colony. This process of swarming, as we describe it, and the process of buying up more land are processes of increasing concern to many young farmers in western Canada, and particularly those that neighbour the colony. The predominant factor in all land deals, as the hon. member for Acadia said last evening, is their ability to pay cash for large tracts of land which, as everyone knows, eliminates most other competitors.
I believe that the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Gundlock) will tell us from past experience that the tracts of land they buy up are usually located in the vicinity of lakes and rivers. In other words, it is usually the best land in our constituencies. The per capita wealth of the residents of the colonies in my constituency alone averages over $3,000 in real estate, to say nothing of other assets.


The colonies are completely lacking in what are considered to be in the outside world intellectual or cultural developments. No books are allowed in the colonies other than those dealing with their own ideas. No musical instruments, radio or television sets are allowed in the colonies. The elders do not even allow trees, flowers or shrubs to be planted around the communal huts in which they live.

At this point, Mr. Speaker, I would like to bring before this house not a repetition of what has been said but rather to point out the effect on the small communities in southern Alberta of this problem. When I say "small communities in southern Alberta" I mean just exactly that, small communities such as my home town, of 500 people, roughly, in an area of 14 or 15 square miles.
Let me take you back to the map of southern Alberta of 15 years ago and point out the number of colonies in that part of the province. You can see the concentration of colonies which existed on five or six thousand acres of the very finest land in Alberta, if not in Canada. I emphasize that this group of colonies is concentrated on these five or six thousand acres of the best land in Canada. It is certainly a rich piece of property.

If you look at the map today you will see the rest of the province dotted with these same colonies at 40-mile intervals. This is what some people call a restriction. While I am on my feet I should like to answer the question raised by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam. He said they do not want anyone to defend them. I would ask the hon. member to find out how much money they have spent by way of fees to lawyers to defend them on this very thing?

I certainly do not want to run afoul of your rulings in any way. However, I think I might say in passing that we had a rather extensive debate a few days ago with respect to the establishment of a joint committee on Indian affairs. During this debate we went extensively into a number of questions confronting Indians, and we went into detail about things with which we hoped the committee might deal when it met. This is the line I was trying to follow when I was suggesting that, inasmuch as we do not know whether or not the committee will deal with the question of absentee balloting or the institution of a system which would allow people to vote who are now denied that right for geographic or economic reasons, it might be proper to express the hope that the committee would deal with it. However, I will not go into any of the details except to say that I hope the committee will deal with this all-important question of absentee balloting.
At the risk of giving you a bit more exercise in rising to make a comment, may I also express my sincere regret that there was not included in the motion some reference to the extremely important question of redistribution. I believe this matter should be dealt with as early as possible, again because of the time element with respect to the census which will probably be completed in the first few months of 1962. If this is the case, then it is safe to assume that that will prevent parliament from dealing with the situations which arise as a result of that census in time for the expected 1962 election, if we follow the four-year period. This matter should be dealt with in order that the 1962 election could be conducted on the basis of up to date redistribution rather than a redistribution that is 10 years old.
I do not believe this is within the scope of the motion, so I had better not run the risk of being told I am out of order. I hope I can express the thought that this subject should have been referred to this committee. I feel it is something we should face up to

as soon as possible, otherwise we will be conducting the 1962 election upon the basis of 1951 statistics which will be completely distorted. Then it will take four or five years more before we can get back to the true situation.
Motion agreed to.

speakeroldname: Hon. George H. Hees (Minister of Transport) moved:
maintopic: RAILWAYS, AIR LINES AND SHIPPING ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMITTEE ON RAILWAYS, AIR LINES AND SHIPPING OWNED AND CONTROLLED BY THE GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
That a sessional committee on railways, air lines and shipping owned and controlled by the government, be appointed to consider the accounts, estimates and bills relating to the Canadian National Railways, the Canadian National (West Indies) Steamships, and Trans-Canada Air Lines, saving always the powers of the committee of supply in relation to the voting of public moneys; and that the said committee be empowered to send for persons, papers and records, and to report from time to time; and that, notwithstanding standing order 67 in relation to the limitation of the number of members, the said committee shall consist of Messrs. Badanai, Bourbonnais, Brassard (Lapointe), Broome, Campeau, Carter, Chevrier, Chown, Creaghan, Drysdale, Fisher, Fraser, Granger, Grills, Horner (Jasper-Edson), Kennedy, Martini, McPhillips, Mc-William, Mitchell, Monteith (Verdun), Pascoe, Robinson, Rowe, Smallwood, Smith (Simcoe North).
He said: Mr. Speaker, this is the usual motion to appoint a sessional committee on railways, air lines and shipping owned and controlled by the government. As the house knows, the committee is for the purpose of considering the affairs of the Canadian National Railways and Trans-Canada Air Lines. If the motion meets with the approval of the house, the annual reports dealing with the two companies will be referred to the committee, together with the items of estimates that are to be reviewed by the committee.
The reports will be ready for tabling tomorrow, and it is planned to have the committee start its sittings on Tuesday, March 29, with the consideration of the reports concerning the Canadian National Railways as the first business.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: RAILWAYS, AIR LINES AND SHIPPING ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMITTEE ON RAILWAYS, AIR LINES AND SHIPPING OWNED AND CONTROLLED BY THE GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think those of us who are familiar with the resolution which comes up annually for consideration and with the manner in which it is dealt with from time to time may perhaps be disappointed in the minister's statement wh'ch was short. In view of the present position of the three government-owned entities it seems to me that the minister might well have taken this opportunity to make a more elaborate statement of the situation, at least in so far as the Canadian National Railways are concerned, to say nothing of Trans-Canada
Railways and Shipping Committee Air Lines. However, beyond making the reflection I have made, I say no more about the matter. I suppose the minister himself is the one who determines what, if any, statement he desires to make.
However, the presentation of this motion enables those of us who sit on this side of the house to give consideration for a moment to the three groups of facilities that are owned and operated by the government and to make certain comments thereon. Obviously it will be at the committee stage when members will have an opportunity of interviewing the various officers of these crown-owned corporations, and to comment and to ask for explanations on the reports as they will be considered from time to time. I do not intend to speak at any length but I want to make some remarks- on the three groups mentioned in the motion for the establishment of this committee, namely the Canadian National Railways, Trans-Canada Air Lines and Canadian National (West Indies) Steamships.
I want first to say something about the Canadian National Railways and to draw the attention of this house to a rather amazing speech made by the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Hamilton) dealing with railway facilities, and more particularly with an aspect which falls under the jurisdiction of this motion. The speech was made on "The Nation's Business" on February 19, 1960 and I hold a copy of it in my hand. At page 2 of the transcript which I have the minister stated the following:
Generally speaking. In the last fifty years, there has not been any new railroad building by government, with the exception of the railway to Churchill and the P.G.E. The provincial governments were busy building roads to meet the needs of the people who lived in their provinces. Therefore, the forward motion of our economic expansion had ceased, and the country was settling down to a consolidating in areas where people lived.
Coming from a minister of the crown this statement, in my opinion, is not only an amazing one but one which is not according to the fact. I will not force the rules of the house by using other expressions. But certainly any member who has sat in this house over a period of years knows full well that there has been substantial building of railway lines or in other words a substantial amount of railroad building over a period of years; and I intend to place on the record what was done in that respect. The Canadian National Railways within a period of 10 years, I believe, built close to some 700 miles of railway lines.
It seems to me that those who make statements of this kind should know what the facts are or, if they do not know, they

Railways and Shipping Committee should not be making statements of this character. What I say now is that I believe it is timely to put on the record the construction initiated by the Canadian National Railways while the Liberal government was in office. I am going to mention eight projects which show clearly that the Canadian National Railways, while we were in office, were not inactive in so far as government railroad building is concerned.
There was first the branch line from Barraute to Kiask Falls or Beattyville, 55 miles of road authorized by parliament in 1946. Next, there was the Sherridon-Lynn Lake branch line in Manitoba, 155 miles in length, authorized by parliament in 1951. Third, there was the line between Terrace and Kitimat, British Columbia, 46 miles in length, authorized by parliament in 1952. Fourth, there were two more lines authorized by parliament in 1954, namely the line between Hillsport and Manitouwadge lake in northern Ontario, 27 miles in length; and the line joining Beattyville, Chibougamau and St. Felicien, 294 miles in length. Fifth, there was a line from Bartibog to Tomogonops river in New Brunswick, 22 miles in length, and authorized by parliament in 1956. Then there were two other projects initiated under the Liberal government in 1957, although approved only at the 1957-58 session of parliament. These were, first, the line from Optic lake to Chisel lake, 52 miles in length and from Sipiwesk to the Burntwood river, 30 miles in length.
I want to point out that this railway building amounted to exactly 681 miles of branch line undertaken by the Canadian National Railways; and in every instance I have mentioned-the eight projects to which I have referred-these lines were built in order to develop national resources in this country, about which the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources should have known, and also built for further development in our country and expansion of the economy. Those were lines built by the Canadian National Railways only. I can, of course, deal only with those in this motion now before the house. As the house knows, other lines were built by companies other than the Canadian National Railways but it would not be proper for me to refer to them at this time. However, 1 hope that when the committee meets there will be an opportunity to inquire from the president of the Canadian National Railways and to obtain from him a statement as to the economic position of these lines and as well of the contribution which these lines are making to the economy of the country as well as to its development.


I have not had time, of course, to examine sufficiently the operations of the Canadian National Railways because, as the minister stated a moment ago, the report has not yet been tabled but will be tabled tomorrow or in the course of a day or two. Nevertheless, it has been possible for me, from other sources, to look at the operations of the Canadian National Railways and unfortunately they are not as good as one might expect them to be. The reports that have been published from month to month indicate that it is evident that the operating revenues for the year will be from $30 million to $40 million less than they were in the peak year of 1956. On the other hand, the operating expenses are going to be a good deal more. As a consequence the net operating income again this year will be insufficient to meet the full amount of the fixed charges.
I draw attention to this fact not for the purpose of being critical of the officers of the Canadian National Railways, for whom, as the house knows, I have the highest regard, but to draw attention to the difficulties and the problems, complex and complicated, that the railways of this country, let alone of the world, have to deal with. This is a problem which must be solved by the government. It is a problem which was brought to our attention when we were on the other side of the house by members of the then opposition. Because it is quite clear to us who have looked at all at this problem that the railways themselves are unable to deal with it; they must be assisted in some form or manner by the government.
Therefore, I do want to urge upon the government the need for early action, and I hope it is already giving consideration to the problem of what is likely to happen when the royal commission report is handed down. While I know that the government cannot anticipate what that report will be, still the government can be thinking now of what some of the problems and some of the solutions are likely to be when the report is handed down. The future of our railways is so closely bound up with the future of Canada that the government must explore every avenue in order to bring remedies and effective means to bear to solve some of the difficult problems facing the railways today.
I said a moment ago that the railways all over the world are in difficult circumstances. That applies perhaps more particularly to those in the United States and in the United Kingdom. We know what a terrific problem the United Kingdom railways face today, but in those two countries there is at least a

greater density of population which we in this country have not got, and that, of course, adds to our difficulties.
Perhaps the most difficult problem, to sum up the matter here at home, is, or appears at least on the face of it to be, insoluble, namely that the costs of operation are continually on the increase while revenues, on the other hand, are more and more limited and restricted. The railways, as the house knows, cannot raise their prices or, to be more exact, their rates, because they are subject to the board of transport commissioners, and because of that they are placed at some disadvantage.
Then again there is always the important problem of co-ordinating the rate with the traffic. It is not a good thing to charge a rate which is as high or higher than the traffic will bear. The increases in freight rates which have been granted from time to time by the board of transport commissioners on the face of them appear unquestionably to be enormous, and they are in fact unquestionably tremendous. But in many cases, as we know, particularly in the central parts of Canada, the whole of these increases cannot be put into effect because of other forms of transportation, other forms of competition, more particularly because of what are known as competitive rates which enter the picture and make it possible for the railways to compete with these other forms of transportation, which thereby deprives them of the full effect of the increases in the rates.
There are, of course, other problems facing the railways with which the minister is as familiar, if not more familiar, as I. There is the question of passenger lines operated at a loss, branch lines operated at a loss, and also the statutory grain rates now before the royal commission and about which I am precluded from speaking.
It may be that the total amount of freight on the railways has increased over the years. I believe the figures will indicate that. But there has not been an increase in the ton-miles of traffic, in other words, in the revenue ton-miles as expressed in rail terms, since the year 1944. This therefore means a loss, because you cannot remain static or at a standstill in an industry such as the railway industry. I agree at once that it is much easier to talk about these problems than to offer solutions to them. I know that because of the experience I had when I sat on the other side of the house.
However, there is now before the royal commission on transportation a number of important problems to which I trust the commission will find a solution. There has already been another royal commission on
Railways and Shipping Committee transportation some years ago, the Turgeon commission. An excellent report was brought in by the commissioner, Mr. Justice Turgeon, and most of the recommendations made in the field of transportation, not to speak of the particular field of railway matters, were implemented by the government of the day. It may well be that those recommendations, even though they were implemented, were not sufficient to meet the problem which is becoming more and more acute and more and more complicated, as I said earlier.
So that I hope, as I am sure most of us on this side of the house do, that it will be possible for the present royal commission to come up with solutions which will be of assistance to the railways. If they do I can assure the minister that they will receive the wholehearted support of those of us who sit on this side of the house.
I want also to take advantage of this motion to bring to the attention of the minister, the government, and more particularly the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker), certain statements which were made in 1957 during the election campaign. At that time very positive promises were given by the Prime Minister that the pension regulations for retired employees would be revised so as to remove existent inequities and anomalies in order to provide a fair and reasonable basic pension. The government has increased pensions to retired civil servants, and I suggest that if it was proper to give them increased pensions, it would be equally proper for the government to carry out the Prime Minister's promises to retired Canadian National Railways' employees.
In case the house has forgotten what some of those promises were, I would like to bring them to the attention of the minister. The Prime Minister spoke on May 4, 1957 at Moncton and Campbellton, and the following is a report in the Toronto Globe and Mail of May 6, 1957:
At both railway centres, the 62-year-old Conservative leader demanded that the C.N.R. should be a model employer. Pensions of $25 a month and less are being received by more than 3,000 retired C.N.R. employees, and many more are not getting enough to live on, he charged.
"How can the government ask other employers to give their men and women benefits when the crown corporations, for which the government is responsible, rewards its faithful employees with pensions like this?" he asked.
Later on at Campbellton on the same day, as reported in the Toronto Globe and Mail of May 6, 1957, the Prime Minister said:
Dealing with labour at his Campbellton meeting, he pledged a Conservative government to:-Revise pension regulations for retired railway employees to remove existent inequities and anomalies and to provide a fair and reasonable basic pension.

Railways and Shipping Committee
I ask the minister when he replies-or perhaps he may ask his parliamentary secretary to reply-to give us some indication as to what consideration the government is giving to these statements made by the Prime Minister. I am sure that when they were made they were made with sincerity but three years have gone by and I think the house is entitled to know what has been done during that time.
I should also like to bring to the attention of the minister a statement made by his colleague who is now the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Monteith) as reported at page 2126 of Hansard of March 12, 1957:
I should like to suggest that the Minister of Transport examine the present inequity of the pensions of employees who were laid off and subsequently rehired, this layoff and subsequent rehiring taking place within the last five or ten years of their service.
That is how one of the colleagues of the present Minister of Transport felt when he sat on this side of the house. How does the Minister of Transport feel with reference to this matter? Does he intend to give

I was almost going to say instructions but I think that would be going too far-does he intend to discuss the matter with his colleagues in the government and also with the officers of the Canadian National Railways with a view to increasing these pensions?
I should like to say a word about lay-offs on the C.N.R. and I am sure the minister will not take me to task in the same manner as he attempted to the other day when I posed a question to him about this. There have been, of course, a substantial number of layoffs in the C.N.R. within the last few months. It has not been possible to get much information on this subject from the minister. He has been evasive. He has avoided the question by asking me a question and of course that has not succeeded in solving very much.
I hold in my hand a press release dated February 10, 1960, which is issued by the Canadian brotherhood of railway transport and general workers and I will read just two paragraphs of it. The first reads:
Recent C.N.R. lay-offs were criticized as "arbitrary" and "possibly wasteful" here today by S. H. Eighteen, chief railway negotiator for the Canadian brotherhood of railway, transport and general workers. Mr. Eighteen made his remarks at a meeting of Brotherhood staff members from across Canada.
He referred particularly to the recent lay-off of upwards of 200 railway employees at Moncton, New Brunswick. "According to the information we have, this action was the result of arbitrary instructions from top management that budget allotments throughout the C.N.R. system be cut by 5 per cent. The lay-offs were not caused by any shortage of work", he said.

It is the second paragraph I should like to bring to the attention of the minister.

I wonder if the hon. member who has the floor would satisfy my difficulty. I am wondering how he relates a discussion of lay-offs on the C.N.R. to the motion to set up the committee. I appreciate that on these motions to set up committees and refer broad issues to them there have in the past developed some very wide debates but according to the strict practice what is relevant in moving to set up a committee is the advisability of having the committee at all and of referring matters to it.
It has been laid down from time to time that if the rules are followed the house should not undertake to debate the matters it is referring to the committee in advance because this results in duplication. I realize that a certain amount of latitude is necessary to discuss a motion of this kind and on some occasions there have been very lengthy debates.
I raise the question not because I quarrel too much with the course the hon. member is taking but to protect myself in the event this debate seeks to broaden out into a discussion of all the affairs of the C.N.R., T.C.A. and other similar organizations.

Mr. Speaker, I agree with you at once that there should not be a general debate which would be of an unending nature because the object of this motion is to discuss many of these matters in committee. I do think, however, there should be allowed enough scope so that a member might discuss a number of items dealing with the three crown corporations that are going to be scrutinized by the committee.
I had almost finished and what I proposed to do was read one other paragraph and then go on to deal with another aspect of the matter. I was going to deal in a general way with a statement that had been made relating to lay-offs on the C.N.R. It seemed to me that that was quite in order provided I did not proceed to take up the lay-offs in each district of the C.N.R. from one end of the country to the other. I should think that would be totally out of order. I was merely going to state the total number of lay-offs referred to in the press release and say I would ask questions on it in the committee, and then proceed to something else.

May I speak to the point of order. I do not think there is any difference

between what I have in mind, what was said by the hon. member for Laurier and what Your Honour has said. I wanted to point out that the next item we are likely to be discussing will be the setting up of the standing committee on agriculture and colonization the motion for which reads:
That the standing committee on agriculture and colonization be empowered to examine and inquire into the delivery of grain by producers to feed mills operating in the designated area as defined by the Canadian Wheat Board Act, and to report to the house observations and proposals thereon.

I realize your difficulties, sir, and will attempt to abide by your decision. I had almost concluded but would like to place on the record the pertinent paragraph in the press release to which I referred:
It was reported to the meeting-
That is, the brotherhood-
-that C.N.R. lay-offs in the first nine months of this year are estimated to number approximately 4,000. A report of the Moncton lay-off was given to the staff conference by Lloyd Abbott, CBRT and GW general chairman, and Ed. McAllister, brotherhood representative, both of Moncton. Mr. Abbott and Mr. McAllister stated that they had met with transport minister George Hees, and that he had promised to take the matter up with Donald Gordon, C.N.R. president.
Railways and Shipping Committee
I think my purpose in discussing this has now been achieved. I would think that the president of the Canadian National Railways should give some indication of what those lay-offs are and where they have taken place. I think the minister will also want to inform the house as to what has been the result of the representations made to Mr. Gordon, in accordance with the statement in this paragraph of the press release.
I now pass on to another matter concerning the Canadian National Railways. I have brought it up on another occasion and I think it is pertinent. I would like to remind the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) that in 1957 it was announced by the then minister of finance in his budget speech that a comprehensive inquiry was being undertaken into transportation conditions in the Atlantic provinces. We all know that a part of this inquiry was to be undertaken by the Canadian National Railways. Three years have now gone by since that time. Would it not be possible to obtain from the minister or from the Canadian National Railways a statement of what has been the result of that inquiry? I think those of us who sit on this side of the house would be entitled not only to know but would like to know what the inquiry resulted in, and I am sure the minister himself would want to take the initiative in telling the house what has transpired, and whether or not any recommendations were made by the Canadian National Railways to the government, and whether those recommendations were implemented.
One of the problems which was of concern to the Liberal government at the time, and still is to the Liberal opposition, is the coastal services of Newfoundland. What conclusions have been reached by the inquiry with regard to those services? Has the government considered all ways and means by which improved services can be given, and perhaps by which better services can be given at a lower cost? What is the government doing to provide additional facilities between Sydney and Port aux Basques? Is the government satisfied that the William Carson is sufficient not only to take care of the traffic that obtains today, but also the traffic that is likely to develop before an additional ferry can be provided? I hope when the committee meets we shall have an opportunity of going into this question.
Before I leave the matter of the operations of the Canadian National Railways I should like to commend the management of the railways for what they have done in this past year to bring about an increase in passenger traffic back to the railways. It is probably not

Railways and Shipping Committee generally realized how much traffic the railways have lost. One must look at the statistics to realize the tremendous amount of competition that there is in this field not only from the air lines but from motor cars as well. The Canadian National Railways, the 22 railways that operate in this country, have been hard pressed to meet that competition.
It is interesting to recall that the number of passengers carried by the railways exceeded 50 million for the first time in 1920 and that, after dropping to 19 million in 1933, the total rose to a record level of 60 million passengers in 1944. But since that time, even during the years of prosperity which we have known, the number has dropped persistently and even discouragingly. In fact, in 1958 the number of passengers had dropped to only 21 million, the same level which existed in 1902.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, it is encouraging to see what the railways are trying to do in an attempt to recapture some of that traffic. They have introduced group fares; they have brought about reduced fares; they have carried on a campaign of advertising which I think has been responsible for restoring in large part the popularity of the railways for passenger traffic; but it is evident that much must be done if the railways are to compete successfully with the air lines, the buses and the highways. I hope it will be possible for the president of the Canadian National Railways to throw some light on this important problem during the course of the committee hearings.
I would like to say a word about the operations of Trans-Canada Air Lines. As I have pointed out on at least three occasions, two of them in this house, the present government has granted traffic rights between Montreal and Chicago to Air France and between Montreal and Chicago to Lufthansa, and therefore has enabled foreign competitors of Trans-Canada Air Lines to provide a direct service between Montreal and Chicago which Trans-Canada Air Lines is unable to offer because the Canadian government has not yet been successful in negotiating a bilateral agreement with the United States which would give Canadian air lines the right to operate a non-stop flight from Montreal to Chicago. I would hope that it would be possible during the committee sittings to obtain information in this respect, to ascertain from Trans-Canada Air Lines whether or not there has been a loss of business in consequence thereof. I should indeed be happy to find that Trans-Canada Air Lines has not lost business. I hope we shall have the opportunity of going into the matter in greater detail.


I would also hope that the committee would be able to see what has been the effect of permitting BOAC to terminate its transAtlantic flights at Malton instead of at Montreal. I think we should have the opportunity of determining what has been the effect of this concession upon the revenues of our own national air lines.
It would appear to me, from what I have already said, and I do not think I am in error, that this concession of granting additional onward rights to the British carrier in Toronto has been a concession which did not receive adequate rights from the other government in return. When we make concessions of this kind it is important that there should always be another exchange of a similar concession; otherwise, it may well be that there will be a reflection in a downward trend of revenues of our own air carriers.
We are naturally concerned with the success of Trans-Canada Air Lines; we are also concerned as taxpayers to make sure that its operations, because of government policy or for some other reason, do not result in a substantial deficit each year.
I pass on now to a discussion of the Canadian National (West Indies) Steamships. I should like to draw to the attention of the government-I am sorry certain hon. members are not in their seats-the attitude taken by these hon. members when they sat on this side of the house in so far as the Canadian National (West Indies) Steamships are concerned. There has been, I have no hesitation in saying, a complete volte-face on the part of the present government in so far as the steamship services between the Federation of the West Indies and Canada are concerned. We know that very strong criticism was expressed in former years of the fact that the fate of the West Indies fleet was uncertain because the government of the day had not made it clear that they intended to carry on this service; and notwithstanding the fact that the government of the day was able to negotiate an extension of those services over a period of five years, it was very severely, vigorously and even bitterly denounced by certain hon. members who now sit on the other side of the house.
The government of the day was fully impressed with the need for services between Canada and the Caribbean and members of the opposition semed to share the government's view; in fact, they felt that the government was not going far enough. I should like to quote here the remarks of the

hon. member for Saint John-Albert (Mr. Bell) made on March 12, 1957. As found at page 2124 of Hansard, he said:
When we get into the committee I hope we shall have not only the lull, complete and polite inquiry we have had in the past, but that we shall also have some strong aggressive leadership on behalf of the government with respect to the future of this very necessary fleet which is an important phase of our life on the east coast.
Is the fleet no longer an important phase of our life on the east coast? What has the member for Saint John-Albert to say now having regard to the statement he made in 1957? The fleet has been liquidated to all intents and purposes. Then there came to his rescue the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan), then the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings. He concurred fully in what the hon. member for Saint John-Albert had to say. I should like to quote what he said as found on page 2127 of Hansard for March 12, 1957:
Therefore I am again emphasizing the importance of strengthening and widening the Canadian National Steamships operating out of Atlantic ports. As the hon. member for Saint John-Albert said, the Caribbean and South America are great potential markets for agricultural and other products of eastern Canada.
Are the markets not there as they were before? What representations has the Minister of National Revenue made to his colleague, the Minister of Transport in respect of this liquidation? What do he and the other member intend to do?
Unfortunately the government has forgotten these brave words and now there is no longer a national service between Canada and the West Indies. All that we have left is an unpleasant recollection of the liquidation by the government of the Canadian National (West Indies) Steamships service. It has merely become an item in the balance sheet of a company that has little more left than corporate existence. I think perhaps I might well add here, and not with tongue in cheek, that the minister sold the Canadian National Steamships fleet to Batista and there are rumours in Montreal that the minister intends now to sell T.C.A. to Castro.
We on this side of the house will support the establishment of this committee. We think its establishment is a good thing. It will allow members of the house and the public at large to get a better idea of the operations of these three crown corporations. It will allow us also to get a reply to some of the questions that are uppermost in our minds and to others which I have put on the record unless, of course, the minister in his reply or his distinguished parliamentary
Railways and Shipping Committee secretary in his reply see fit to comment on these matters. We on this side of the house will support the motion.

Mr. Speaker, it is only a few days ago that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees\ speaking in a debate on civic aviation that had some relevance to this motion, made a general comment that I suppose is rather close to his heart and sums up his feelings about his responsibilities as Minister of Transport. He said, as found at page 1855 of Hansard:
-I would simply say that private enterprise has built the Canadian economy and will continue to expand it. There is no place for the stultifying influence of socialist policies in this or any other industry in Canada-
The reason I mention this is partly that the minister is the head of the fastest growing department of the government. It is burgeoning all over the place. For a free enterpriser he has more civil servants lining up under him than anyone else. He also happens to be the minister responsible for these public enterprises, Canadian National, T.C.A. and so on, which can hardly be called private.
I have often wondered how in cabinet meeting the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) arrived at picking someone for this ministry who by his very statements seems so wrong for the job. He is a private enterpriser, a free enterpriser and proud of it but he is the one who is responsible for these public organizations. This is the reason why I lead off with some doubts about the career of these crown corporations when they are under the aegis of this particular minister. The fact that he also has more civil servants behind him than any other minister is an indication of the paradox in his position.
When I finally landed in the great big city of Toronto after coming from a small town in the bush and settled down in central Toronto I used to walk to school and pass a big factory called the George Hees factory. I also happened to see the minister playing football and I realized that he had a very prominent part to play in Toronto. I think that position and background explain the beliefs that he put on the record last week.
Because I am a small town boy from a C.N.R. family I have always had a great loyalty to Canadian National Railways. After all, it put the bread and butter in the mouths of the members of our family. From growing up in a C.N.R. town and now, in having four divisional points in my constituency I know there is a considerable amount of pride in the organization and a feeling that a public organization like the C.N.R. can do a good job and as good or better job than this imaginary private enterprise about which the minister talks.

Railways and Shipping Committee
Of course, when you talk to C.N.R. people you find that the railway could probably be doing a much more excellent job if it had not been created in order to bail out private enterprise. I think the minister will recognize that was the case if he goes back to the events that led to the creation of Canadian National Railways. It was the politicians' way at that time, the way of private enterprisers like the minister, to get a bunch of bond and debenture holders and shareholders out of a very difficult situation, and so the Canadian National was born. Now we have it under the responsibility, though not directly, of a minister who does not believe in this kind of enterprise at all and in a paradoxical way has already given an indication so far as T.C.A. is concerned.
At the present time Canadian National Railways also happens to be headed by a man who is supremely dedicated to free enterprise and the private enterprise approach. Last year when he was before the committee, toward the end of very long and weary proceedings-I am not ashamed of the fact that I took up a great deal of the time of the committee-I said to Mr. Gordon, as found at page 210 of the proceedings of the committee:
Several times during the two hearings the president has said that there are difficulties raised by his appearance before this committee. Have you any suggestions that you could make which would make the task easier for you and at the same time not inhibit or limit the parliamentary inquiry?
Mr. Gordon came back with that blunt frankness of his and said:
That is a great temptation for me. With the greatest deference, I should be glad to express my views in regard to this committee's work.
That is the committee that is coming up. He said:
With great deference, and with no suggestion to restrict the rights of members of parliament-
I should like to interject here that sometimes I think, when I hear that phrase, "with great deference", that he has been listening to the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier). I have noticed that is a pel phrase of his.
-it seems to me in connection with my 10 years' experience, that more and more we are losing sight of the fact that the Canadian National Railways is a highly competitive organization, and its management should be designed along the lines of a private enterprise organization.
Here is the head of the Canadian National Railways calling for a private enterprise type of organization. Of course, the first thing that this brings into my mind, if you understand that the members of the committee represent the shareholders, is that I should like to see the directors at this meeting so

that we, the shareholders, can quiz the directors. After all, a private enterprise has its president, but it also has directors. This is one of the things I want to suggest in connection with this committee, that we not only have Mr. Gordon and all his employed experts, but we also have a look at these directors who are working in association with Mr. Gordon and with the minister to make the Canadian National Railways a going concern.
As a result of my experience in this committee I would say we certainly need to do something about getting a better look at Canadian National Railways. I should like to suggest also that in so far as members of parliament are concerned and in so far as Canadian National Railways is concerned, there is a conflict here between the C.N.R. as an enterprise and a member's responsibility to his constituency and to the employees of the Canadian National Railways. The Canadian National is not a private enterprise, even if it is in some kind of restricted and heavily regulated competition with the Canadian Pacific and other railways. It is a government corporation. I think this explains why Mr. Gordon finds the committee so frustrating and why a number of the members of the committee find Mr. Gordon so frustrating.
I want to make the point here that this year I hope the committee will do a better job, that is that it will stick more to policy and be less concerned about details such as whether a certain railway station needs a new urinal. Mr. Gordon also has to realize, and I think the minister can put it over to him, that the reason members of parliament nag about such questions as the effect of automation and the whole business of job security is that these are the bread and butter things that are brought to them.
I see the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Benidickson) is in the house, I do not like to draw an example from his constituency, particularly, but perhaps he will forgive me in this particular case. On April 24 the Canadian National Railways will commence its springtime card. It has decided, in its wisdom, and I suppose in the interests of efficiency, that for the first time on western lines it is going to run its freight over two divisions. This is a revolutionary move. This is a consequence of the tremendous expenditure in central traffic control.

I insist that this is the wrong approach at this time in the 60's. It is wrong to go along to within a month or two months of the time and suddenly let a community know that this is it. I insist, too, that with the scope of the research organization Canadian National has there is no excuse for this kind of delay in letting communities, employees and unions know the facts on where they stand.
There are a number of items which I believe we should bring up before this committee in terms of general policy. I make no apology for the fact that they do not relate to the larger problem to which the hon. member for Laurier was referring before he got off into the 1957 election promises, who said what, and why and where. The hon. member was stressing the fact that the railway industry in Canada is in a very bad way; that we have a royal commission sitting, and that we need real leadership in order to resolve these problems. I should like to say that the points with which I should like to see the committee deal relate to the human problems of the communities, the workers, their unions, their organizations and their relationships with Canadian National Railways. We still do not know the scope of the retraining program that the Canadian National plans to carry out. I believe that
Railways and. Shipping Committee can be fairly said. We do not know what the unions and the railway are doing. I am not speaking as a union defender in this case. We do not know what changes have been negotiated in the union agreements or are being negotiated that would encourage retraining and a wider transfer of employees with long service from one union jurisdiction to another.
We have one example in my constituency of a man who has worked for 29 years as a machinist. He was laid off and no other job was available in Canadian National Railways. It seems to me that there is a failure in the whole union-management relationship when you find a situation like this.

One of the things I think we should have so far as the future is concerned, is a clear indication from Mr. Gordon as to whether or not he believes there is featherbedding on the Canadian National Railways. I think he needs to spell that out. If there is, I should like to know in what areas of the operations of Canadian National there is this featherbedding. I should like to know why the Canadian National has not produced studies to show the cost of featherbedding, if there is any. I think it is much less than a lot of rumours would indicate. I believe it is a problem that needs a great deal of understanding and sympathy, and also a very definite attempt to resolve.
I should like to know what the position of Mr. Gordon and the Canadian National is in so far as compulsory arbitration of wage disputes is concerned, especially as recommended to the government by the Canadian railway association. If the railway is in favour, what is the yardstick the Canadian National Railways wants to use for the determination of wages? What do they want the arbitrator to look at? Is it the white goods industry? Where are we going to get our pattern for the railway workers until we know the answers to these questions?
I think we need to know what the Canadian National Railways feels about this question of job security, severance pay, expenses for moving and shifting people as a result of the dislocation that has come with the advances the railways are making. It seems to me these are the questions on the human side about which Canadian National Railways should be much more concerned. Mr. Gordon, in his statement last year in the committee, when he was challenged to make suggestions, said:
The minute details which each member has gone into is a matter of interest, but they do not touch upon the question they should be interested in

Railways and Shipping Committee
and that is: Is the management of the C.N.R. an efficient management, or otherwise; and if you come to the conclusion it is not, for God's sake tell us and fire the lot of us. Take the general approach to it and let us work as a private enterprise corporation and manage it as such. Put us on the spot. Challenge us.
Again I suggest that Mr. Gordon's conception of private enterprise, if the C.N.R. may be considered to be a private enterprise, may be all due fact. But how can he seriously ask us to look at the Canadian National Railways as an efficient organization when built right into our transportation structure in Canada we have these continuing losses.
The Canadian National Railways in the foreseeable future, under the present setup, is never going to have a surplus. That is not a wild statement. Until it can be cleared out and other railways can be cleared out of its passenger operations, out of its branch line operations that are not making good, we are not going to get to the stage where we can look at the railways as a private enterprise operation. I think we could have a president every year and fire him every year and we would not get a balanced budget for the Canadian National Railways or any attractive kind of profit structure.
I suggest that one of the things the committee should be looking for from Mr. Gordon are his views on where the Canadian National Railways should go, or in what direction we should go, in the light of the drastic situation in which the railways find themselves. I think this putting up of the idea "Let us look at it as a private enterprise" is nonsense in relation to the situation the railways are in. But if we are going to accept this suggestion, since the majority members of the committee are followers of our free enterprise minister, it might not be a bad idea for them and Mr. Gordon to consider and to recommend abolishing the board of transport commissioners. Abolish all these regulations and let us have a dog fight. Let us get down to the basic question as to whether in a true private enterprise ethos, the railways can survive or how much of them will be left.
That is the choice the minister and the Conservative members have if they are logical in their private enterprise view. Let us put it up. Let us get rid of all these regulations that are hampering this mollycoddling of employees as some people seem to think. Let us get down to a real tough operation, a free enterprise operation. Then Mr. Gordon can be consistent with his approach.
I do not think we shall come to that point. I do not think it is the right approach. But we certainly need to get away from this conception of looking at the Canadian National


Railways and Trans-Canada Air Lines as an image of a private organization. We are not going to get to grips in this committee with the big issue that is involved in railroading pointed out by the hon. member for Laurier, namely where is this government going with its transportation policy.
I really wish I could believe the minister when he talks about private enterprise and says that none of this monopoly, or vested interest is for him. If he really believes in that, I think he should act in that way and so should the government. This is the challenge. This is why many people voted for him. It certainly seems to me that at least it would be consistent to do so.
But what I am afraid is going to happen is that they are going to continue to muddle along with this halfway system, with no confidence in the public corporation; that the whole thing is going to go by default; that the mess is going to get greater and that we shall probably have another royal commission in another year or two. For that reason I certainly would support the hon. member for Laurier in looking forward to hearing from the minister right now on questions such as this or from the erstwhile parliamentary secretary.
One of the things that I wanted to touch on and which I think comes in logically here, although the Speaker may take some objection, is the question relating to the fleet that was sold and the role of Mr. Hal Banks of the S.I.U. in the causes of such sale. One year, when before our parliamentary committee Mr. Gordon, the president of the Canadian National Railways, admitted that he was to some degree responsible for bringing Mr. Banks to Canada. I think it was Mr. Gordon and the Liberal government who brought in Mr. Banks. Now that we have him, we are stuck with him. One of the things I want pointed out to this committee is just where Mr. Banks stands with regard to these government operations.

I can assure all hon. members that in each case the lay-offs in question are gone into thoroughly and that every effort is made by the management to see that the men are kept on if possible. If it is not available, then they are re-employed as soon as possible.
I can assure all hon. members of the house that both the management of the C.N.R. and this government are very disturbed any time it is necessary to lay off even one man. When a man loses his job it is a very serious thing, and not only does he lose employment but it also has a very demoralizing effect upon him, particularly if the lay-off is of any duration. I can assure hon. members that the management of the C.N.R. and this government will do everything possible to make it unnecessary for people to be laid off, but if it is absolutely necessary, we will do everything possible to get them into another job, or back on the job as soon as we can.

Railways and Shipping Committee
